sentences.text: Diabloceratops was a medium-sized, quadrupedal herbivore that grew up to 4.5 meters in length and weighed 1.3 metric tons, though some estimates suggest it could reach 5.5 meters.
The name Diabloceratops means "devil-horned face", derived from the Spanish word for devil and the Greek term for horned face.

The type specimen consists of a partial skull with part of the lower jaw, where the right side is intact but the left side is weathered, and the animal possessed a pair of very long spikes on its frill.
Diabloceratops possessed an accessory opening in the skull that is reduced or absent in later, more advanced ceratopsids, a feature also found in the Protoceratopsidae.
At the time of its discovery, Diabloceratops was the oldest-known ceratopsid and the first centrosaurine found south of Montana.
The species Diabloceratops eatoni was named and described in 2010 by James Ian Kirkland and Donald DeBlieux, establishing the genus Diabloceratops.
Only two specimens of Diabloceratops eatoni have been found in the Last Chance Creek Member of the Wahweap Formation in Kane County, Utah.
The holotype specimen UMNH VP 16699 was collected by Don DeBlieux in 2002 from intraclastic sandstone deposited during the Campanian stage of the Cretaceous.
A second specimen, UMNH VP 16704, was discovered in 1998 by Joshua A. Smith and assigned to Diabloceratops in 2010.
Both specimens are currently housed in the collection of the Utah Natural History Museum.
Diabloceratops shared its environment with hadrosaurs, lambeosaurs, ankylosaurs, pachycephalosaurs, and the theropod Lythronax argestes, likely the apex predator.
A unique fossil trackway discovered in 2010 includes mammalian den complexes and digging grooves presumably made by a maniraptoran dinosaur.

Subsequent phylogenetic analyses continue to classify Diabloceratops as a basal centrosaurine, a basal genus within the Centrosaurinae subfamily of the family Ceratopsidae, within the class Ornithischia.
Kirkland noted that Diabloceratops shared characteristics with the more "primitive" Protoceratopsidae.

Diabloceratops lived at the end of the Cretaceous Period, approximately 79.9 million years ago during the Campanian, in what is now North America, when the Western Interior Seaway was at its widest extent.
The habitat of Diabloceratops included lakes, floodplains, and east-flowing rivers.
Some researchers suggest that specimen UMNH VP 16704 is more similar to Machairoceratops, Yehuecauhceratops, and Menefeeceratops than to Diabloceratops due to the fan-shaped end of the squamosal.
